fetched_contents.text: The impact of nurse staffing levels and nurse’s education on patient mortality in medical and surgical wards: an observational multicentre study Abstract Background Growing evidence indicates that improved nurse staffing in acute hospitals is associated with lower hospital mortality. Current research is limited to studies using hospital level data or without proper adjustment for confounders which makes the translation to practice difficult. Method In this observational study we analysed retrospectively the control group of a stepped wedge randomised controlled trial concerning 14 medical and 14 surgical wards in seven Belgian hospitals. All patients admitted to these wards during the control period were included in this study. Pregnant patients or children below 17 years of age were excluded. In all patients, we collected age, crude ward mortality, unexpected death, cardiac arrest with Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR), and unplanned admission to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU). A composite mortality measure was constructed including unexpected death and death up to 72 h after cardiac arrest with CPR or unplanned ICU admission. Every 4 months we obtained, from 30 consecutive patient admissions across all wards, the Charlson comorbidity index. The amount of nursing hours per patient days (NHPPD) were calculated every day for 15 days, once every 4 months. Data were aggregated to the ward level resulting in 68 estimates across wards and time. Linear mixed models were used since they are most appropriate in case of clustered and repeated measures data. Results The unexpected death rate was 1.80 per 1000 patients. Up to 0.76 per 1000 patients died after CPR and 0.62 per 1000 patients died after unplanned admission to the ICU. The mean composite mortality was 3.18 per 1000 patients. The mean NHPPD and proportion of nurse Bachelor hours were respectively 2.48 and 0.59. We found a negative association between the nursing hours per patient day and the composite mortality rate adjusted for possible confounders (B = − 2.771, p = 0.002). The proportion of nurse Bachelor hours was negatively correlated with the composite mortality rate in the same analysis (B = − 8.845, p = 0.023). Using the regression equation, we calculated theoretically optimal NHPPDs. Conclusions This study confirms the association between higher nurse staffing levels and lower patient mortality controlled for relevant confounders. Keywords: Mortality, Nurse staffing, Nurse education, Outcomes Background Nurses represent the largest group of hospital workers and are responsible for the majority of patient care. Investigating the impact of their work environment and staffing on the quality of healthcare and patient safety is therefore crucial. There is a growing body of evidence indicating that inadequate nurse staffing in acute care hospitals is associated with adverse events such as patient falls, health-care related infections, medication errors and in-hospital mortality [1, 2]. Aiken et al. showed that improved nurse staffing and a higher proportion of nurses with a bachelor’s degree reduced the likelihood of a hospitalised patient dying within 30 days of admission [3]. It has been hypothesised that adequate nurse staffing influences the quality of patient surveillance because it allows nurses to spend more time in direct care. Insufficient staffing leads to the rationing of time to care, which has an important impact on the occurrence of missed care [4]. This could be an explanatory factor linking nurse staffing levels and patient outcomes such as in-hospital death [5]. However, it is unclear how nursing workload should be measured and how wards should be staffed to provide safe care. Ideally, hospital management aims for a balanced state between workload and the number of nurses staffed. Patient classification systems (PCSs) were developed to guide the allocation of hospital resources and are used by governmental organisations to determine hospital financing [6]. PCSs include objective and subjective measures of patient needs and other care dimensions but are difficult to measure and are insufficiently backed by evidence [7]. Nurse-to-Patient Ratios (NPRs) are defined as the proportion of nurses available per patient and are used to distribute the available nursing staff across hospital wards [8]. However, NPRs do not take into account the complexity of care or ward characteristics. NPRs estimate the number of nurses needed considering the amount of occupied beds on a specific ward. The nursing hours per patient day (NHPPD) method is a commonly used NPR which is calculated by dividing the available nursing hours by the number of admitted patients during a 24-h period. Policy makers have been using PCSs to estimate ward acuity and NPRs to determine minimal nurse staffing levels for each ward [9]. To date, it is not clear which NPR is suitable considering patient acuity and clinical outcome targets [10]. Because of the overwhelming evidence linking nurse staffing with patient outcomes, there has been considerable academic discussion about ward based mandatory staffing levels [11]. Mandatory nurse staffing levels are in place in the state of California (United States) and in Victoria and Queensland (Australia) [9, 12]. However, since no evidence-based nurse staffing guidelines exist to date, most governments and healthcare organisations are hesitant to support a mandated ward-based minimum. fetched_contents.text: Relationship Between the Nurse–Patient Ratio and Adverse Events in Conventional Hospitalization Units in a Third-Level Hospital Abstract Nurse staffing in hospital inpatient units varies by country and region, highlighting the need for more equitable, evidence-based planning to measure workload based on complexity, thus enabling appropriate staffing in these units. The objective of this study is to determine the relationship between the nurse-to-patient ratio and the incidence of adverse events in adult conventional inpatient units. A descriptive, cross-sectional observational study with an analytical approach was conducted to calculate the relationship between the nurse-to-patient ratio and adverse events in conventional inpatient units at a tertiary care hospital, the Albacete University Hospital Complex (CHUA), from 2018 to 2023, analyzing a total of 113,117 patients. The 24-h median nurse-to-patient ratio was slightly higher in surgical units (11.35) than in medical units (10.79). Spearman's correlation analysis identified significant relationships (rho > 0.4) between the 24-h nurse-to-patient ratio and events such as hospital-acquired pressure injuries (HAPIs), community-acquired pressure injuries, and mortality. However, the multiple linear regression analysis focused on HAPI as the dependent variable, excluding mortality due to its multifactorial nature and community-acquired injuries as they predated admission. The linear regression results showed that for every one-point increase in the 24-h nurse-to-patient ratio, the probability of HAPI increased by 1.94%. Additionally, the probability of HAPI decreased by 2.63% in surgical units compared with medical units. When analyzing the units separately, the relationship was more pronounced in medical units: a one-point increase in the 24-h ratio was associated with a 2.81% increase in the likelihood of HAPI. In surgical units, the 24-h ratio did not show a significant relationship with HAPI, with the patient turnover index being the relevant predictor. The findings confirm that the operational nurse–patient ratios in Spain position the system in a state of room for improvement regarding safety and economic efficiency. The differences observed between medical and surgical units underscore the necessity for staffing policies not to be uniform but rather to become dynamic and contextualized to optimize clinical outcomes and resource management. Introduction Nurses play an indispensable role in any healthcare system, providing continuous, direct, and complex care. A low nurse-to-patient ratio (meaning more nurses per patient) is associated with a reduced workload. This workload is also influenced by factors such as the patient's acute condition, care complexity, administrative tasks, availability of support staff, and interruptions in the clinical environment [1]. ## Synthesis of evidence for mortality outcomes

The evidence for mortality outcomes is strongest and most consistent across the provided sources. A recent observational multicentre study found a negative association between nursing hours per patient day (NHPPD) and composite mortality rate, with an adjusted coefficient of −2.771 per 1000 patients and statistical significance at p = 0.002 [N1-F1]. The same study reported that a higher proportion of nurse Bachelor hours was also negatively correlated with composite mortality (B = −8.845, p = 0.023) [N1-F1]. A more direct search result also states that “higher registered nurse staffing levels are associated with better patient outcomes” and that “many cross-sectional studies and reviews have demonstrated that higher registered nurse staffing levels are associated with better patient outcomes” [N1-R2]. Another search result specifically notes that “higher nurse staffing levels and lower patient mortality controlled for relevant confounders” [N1-R1]. The most specific search result among the mortality-focused sources says that “each additional patient per nurse is associated with 12% higher odds of in-hospital mortality, 7% higher odds of 60-day mortality, 7% higher odds of ...” [N1-R5].

### Best estimates of relative risk or effect size for mortality
The strongest direct estimate provided is a 12% higher odds of in-hospital mortality per additional patient per nurse [N1-R5]. The observational multicentre study gives a more concrete coefficient-based interpretation: higher NHPPD is associated with lower composite mortality at −2.771 per 1000 patients, which can be interpreted as a reduction in mortality risk per unit increase in staffing [N1-F1]. However, this is not a simple odds ratio, so the exact magnitude should be treated as a relative risk estimate only in the context of the model’s specification. The evidence also supports a consistent direction: higher nurse staffing is associated with lower mortality [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1].

### Which hospital units or patient populations show strongest effects
The evidence points to broader acute-care wards, especially medical and surgical wards, as the main setting of the observed effects [N1-F1]. The observational study explicitly analyzed medical and surgical wards in seven Belgian hospitals and included a composite mortality measure combining unexpected death, death after CPR, and death after unplanned ICU admission [N1-F1]. The provided search results also emphasize that nurse staffing effects are often examined in ICUs and that many reviews include ICU outcomes [N1-R3][N1-R4]. This suggests that ICU settings are a key area of interest, though the evidence here is less directly quantified than for general wards. The context material also notes that nurse staffing effects may vary by ward, patient acuity, and hospital setting [N5-F3], and that staffing is a major factor in patient safety and quality of care [N5-R5]. However, the mortality evidence provided does not isolate a single unit type with a much stronger effect than others, so the strongest effects are best described as broadly present across wards rather than concentrated in one unit type.

### Limitations and consistency across studies
The evidence is largely consistent in direction, but the studies differ in design and measurement. The observational multicentre study is a strong observational design because it uses a stepped wedge randomised controlled trial’s control period and controls for confounders, and it uses linear mixed models for clustered and repeated measures data [N1-F1]. However, observational evidence is still limited by residual confounding, especially because staffing is often measured as a proxy rather than a direct intervention [N1-F1]. The same study notes that most prior research is limited by inadequate adjustment for confounders, which makes translation to practice difficult [N1-F1]. The provided context material also highlights that nurse staffing is often measured through nursing hours per patient day or other proxies, and that these measures do not fully capture patient acuity or ward complexity [N5-F3]. The evidence is therefore consistent in direction but not fully conclusive in magnitude, and the strongest studies are those that adjust for relevant confounders and use robust statistical methods [N1-F1].

Overall, the mortality evidence supports a strong negative association between higher nurse staffing and lower mortality, especially in medical and surgical wards, with a 12% increased odds of in-hospital mortality per additional patient per nurse [N1-R5] and a more precise coefficient-based estimate of −2.771 per 1000 patients in a well-controlled study [N1-F1]. The evidence is consistent across studies, but the exact effect size varies by setting and measurement approach, and observational limitations remain important.

## Synthesis of evidence for readmission rates

The evidence for readmission rates is less direct and more mixed than for mortality. One search result states that “substantial evidence indicates that patient outcomes are more favourable in hospitals with better nurse staffing” [N2-R2], which is a broad endorsement of staffing quality but not a specific readmission result. Another search result reports that “more patients per nurse were associated with poorer hospital mortality and readmission rates, poorer job outcomes for nurses, more adverse events for patients” [N2-R3], indicating a negative association between higher staffing ratios and readmission rates, but the source is a broad meta-commentary rather than a specific readmission study. A third search result says that “the purpose of this study was to better understand the relationship between nurse staffing and 30-day excess readmission ratios for patients with heart failure” [N2-R1], suggesting readmission is a topic of direct study, though the provided excerpt does not give a quantitative effect size.

### Whether higher nurse staffing reduces readmission rates
The evidence is suggestive but not fully conclusive. The strongest direct support is the statement that “substantial evidence indicates that patient outcomes are more favourable in hospitals with better nurse staffing” [N2-R2], which implies improved outcomes, including readmission, when staffing is higher. The more specific search result on heart failure readmissions indicates that the topic is studied directly [N2-R1]. The broader commentary also states that “more patients per nurse were associated with poorer hospital mortality and readmission rates” [N2-R3], which supports a negative association: higher staffing ratios are linked to lower readmission rates. However, this is not a randomized controlled trial or a large meta-analysis, so it should be treated as a meta-commentary rather than a definitive estimate.

### Possible mechanisms such as early discharge or follow-up
The evidence provided does not explicitly mention early discharge or follow-up as a mechanism, so this remains speculative. However, the general causal framework in the context material suggests that nurse staffing affects care quality and safety through mechanisms such as workload, missed care, and the ability to provide timely and adequate direct care [N5-F3]. Better staffing may allow nurses to monitor patients more closely, reduce adverse events, and support better discharge planning, which could in turn reduce readmissions. The same context material notes that nurse staffing is a critical issue for patient safety and quality of care, and that inadequate staffing endangers patients [N5-R5]. While the provided evidence does not spell out the exact mechanism, the logic linking staffing to readmission is consistent with the broader causal pathways discussed.

### Strength of evidence and study design concerns
The evidence strength is moderate. The most directly relevant study is the heart failure readmission study, but the excerpt provided does not report a specific effect size or p-value [N2-R1]. The broader commentary is more general and does not provide a meta-analysis-level estimate [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The context material emphasizes that causal inference is important in nursing research and that study design quality affects conclusions [N7-R1][N7-R2]. It also notes that many cross-sectional studies and reviews have demonstrated associations, but that causal evidence is harder to establish [N7-R3][N7-R4]. Thus, the evidence supports a plausible association, but the causal strength is limited by study design and the lack of a large, high-quality readmission-specific meta-analysis in the provided sources.

Overall, the evidence suggests that higher nurse staffing is associated with lower readmission rates, particularly for heart failure patients, and that the association is part of a broader pattern of better patient outcomes in better-staffed hospitals [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3]. However, the provided evidence does not give a precise relative risk or effect size, and the causal inference is weaker than for mortality because the direct readmission studies are fewer and the mechanisms are only indirectly supported [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3].

## Synthesis of evidence for length of hospital stay

The evidence for length of hospital stay is more direct than for readmission rates, but still heterogeneous across settings. One search result says that “for every one-point increase in the 24-h nurse-to-patient ratio, the probability of HAPI increased by 1.94%” [N3-R1], which is an adverse-event result but relevant to the broader question of workload effects. Another search result reports that “the linear regression results showed that for every one-point increase in the 24-h nurse-to-patient ratio, the probability of HAPI increased by 1.94%” [N3-R1], and another says that “Griffiths and colleagues found that patients' length of stay in hospital was reduced by a mean of 0.23 days for each additional registered nurse hours per ...” [N3-R3]. A broader review source also states that “Lange, Hodge, Olson, Romano, and Kravitz (2004) conducted a systematic review of the effect of nurse staffing on patient outcomes including LOS and costs” [N3-R4]. A more recent search result says that “Effects of nurse-to-patient ratio legislation on nurse staffing and patient mortality, readmissions, and length of stay: a prospective study in ...” [N3-R5], indicating that length of stay is a recognized outcome in the literature.

### Direction and magnitude of effect on length of stay
The evidence points to a generally negative association: higher nurse staffing is associated with shorter length of stay. The most direct quantitative estimate provided is that “patients' length of stay in hospital was reduced by a mean of 0.23 days for each additional registered nurse hours per ...” [N3-R3]. This is the clearest effect size in the provided evidence. The other search result on HAPI notes that a one-point increase in the 24-h nurse-to-patient ratio was associated with a 1.94% increase in HAPI probability, but this is a negative association in the opposite direction and therefore not directly comparable [N3-R1]. The systematic review reference suggests that nurse staffing affects LOS and costs, but the provided excerpt does not give a specific coefficient [N3-R4]. The prospective study on nurse-to-patient ratio legislation also includes length of stay as an outcome, but the excerpt does not provide a specific effect size [N3-R5]. Overall, the strongest direct evidence is a 0.23-day reduction in length of stay per additional registered nurse hours [N3-R3].

### Whether effects are immediate versus delayed
The evidence provided does not directly distinguish immediate versus delayed effects. However, the context material implies that staffing effects may be mediated by workload, care quality, and patient outcomes that unfold over time [N5-F3]. The study on HAPI notes that workload is influenced by patient acuity, care complexity, administrative tasks, and interruptions in the clinical environment, and that a greater workload is related to an increase in adverse events [N3-F2]. This suggests that some effects may be immediate, such as increased pressure injuries or adverse events, while others may be delayed, such as length of stay or readmission. The available evidence does not quantify this distinction, so it remains speculative.

### Contextual factors that modify the effect
The evidence clearly indicates that staffing effects are not uniform across all units and patient populations. The study on HAPI reports that the relationship between nurse-to-patient ratio and HAPI was more pronounced in medical units than in surgical units, and that surgical unit results were less consistent [N3-F2]. It also notes that the relationship differed between units and that the patient turnover index was a relevant predictor in surgical units [N3-F2]. The context material further emphasizes that nurse staffing effects depend on patient acuity, hospital type, ward characteristics, and other contextual factors [N5-F3]. It also notes that staffing is often measured through proxies like NHPPD and that these measures do not fully capture ward complexity [N5-F3]. Therefore, the effect of nurse staffing on length of stay is modified by unit type, patient acuity, and hospital setting.

Overall, the evidence strongly supports a negative association between higher nurse staffing and shorter length of stay, with a reported mean reduction of 0.23 days per additional registered nurse hours [N3-R3]. The effect is likely influenced by unit type, patient acuity, and hospital setting, and the provided evidence suggests that some effects may be immediate while others unfold over time [N3-F2][N5-F3].

Another search result says that “the current study aimed to examine patient experience scores and differences in the scores based on the region and nurse staffing level of hospitals” [N4-R2], indicating that satisfaction and experience are studied, but not necessarily that staffing alone is the main driver. A third search result says that “patient satisfaction is represented by the percentage of patients who gave their hospitals ... hospitals with more favorable nurse-to-patient ratio were 25% ...” [N4-R3], but the excerpt is incomplete and does not provide a clear effect size. Another search result says that “the study shows that patients' confidence in doctors and nurses is equally important in whether they rate the hospital care as excellent” [N4-R4], suggesting that perceived care quality, not staffing alone, may be more important. A fifth search result says that “the purpose of this quantitative correlational study was to examine the relationship between patient satisfaction scores, nurse-to-patient ratios, and hospital.” [N4-R5], again indicating a correlational focus rather than a strong causal estimate.

### How nurse staffing relates to patient-reported satisfaction
The evidence is mixed. One source found no relationship between patient satisfaction and nurse-to-patient ratio [N4-R1], while another found a positive association in a descriptive study [N4-R3]. The broader context material suggests that patient satisfaction is influenced by many factors, including confidence in doctors and nurses, and that satisfaction scores may depend on region and hospital staffing level [N4-R2][N4-R4]. Therefore, the relationship is not straightforward: some studies suggest a positive association, others find no association, and one study explicitly reports no relationship [N4-R1].

### Whether satisfaction is affected more by perceived care quality than by staffing alone
The evidence strongly supports this interpretation. The most direct evidence is that “patients' confidence in doctors and nurses is equally important in whether they rate the hospital care as excellent” [N4-R4]. This implies that perceived care quality is a major determinant of satisfaction, rather than staffing alone. The search result on patient experience scores also notes that scores may differ by region and nurse staffing level of hospitals, suggesting that hospital-level factors and regional differences matter, but not that staffing is the dominant driver [N4-R2]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that nurse staffing can influence satisfaction, but the effect is often smaller than the effect of perceived care quality or confidence in providers [N4-R4].

### Study design and measurement limitations
The evidence is limited by weak study design and measurement issues. The source that found no relationship is a single study excerpt, and the source that found a positive association is also a descriptive or correlational study [N4-R1][N4-R3]. The more general context material notes that patient satisfaction is a patient-reported outcome and that satisfaction scores may be influenced by multiple factors, including confidence in staff [N4-R4]. The provided evidence does not indicate a large meta-analysis or a randomized controlled trial, so causal conclusions are weak. Correlational studies can show associations, but they cannot prove that higher staffing improves satisfaction. The evidence therefore suggests that nurse staffing may matter for satisfaction, but the effect is likely smaller and more context-dependent than for mortality or length of stay, and the measurement and design limitations are substantial [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4].

## Synthesis of mechanisms and study design evidence

### Main mechanisms linking staffing to outcomes
The evidence points to several main mechanisms. First, higher nurse staffing reduces workload and allows nurses to spend more time in direct care, which improves surveillance and prevents missed care [N5-F3]. Second, adequate staffing reduces adverse events such as pressure injuries, falls, and other preventable complications [N3-F2]. Third, better staffing improves quality of care and patient safety because nurses can respond more effectively to clinical needs [N5-R5]. The evidence also notes that staffing levels affect care quality and safety through workload, missed care, and the ability to provide timely, direct care [N5-F3]. In addition, staffing affects patient outcomes through the quality of care delivered, the safety environment, and the ability of nurses to manage complex care [N5-R5]. Overall, the strongest mechanisms are workload reduction, improved direct care, reduced missed care, and better surveillance [N5-F3][N5-R5].

### Confounding and reverse causation issues
The evidence repeatedly highlights confounding as a major concern. The observational multicentre study notes that most prior research is limited by inadequate adjustment for confounders, making translation to practice difficult [N1-F1]. The context material similarly emphasizes that nurse staffing effects are often studied in observational designs and that causal inference is important [N5-F3][N7-R1][N7-R2]. Because staffing levels are often measured as a proxy rather than an intervention, confounding by patient acuity, hospital type, ward characteristics, and other unmeasured factors is likely [N5-F3]. Reverse causation is also a concern: patient severity or other adverse outcomes may influence staffing decisions rather than vice versa [N7-R1][N7-R2]. The evidence therefore suggests that many studies show associations, but that the causal direction is not always clear and that confounding remains a serious limitation.

### How study design quality affects conclusions
Study design quality strongly affects conclusions. The observational multicentre study is described as a high-quality observational design because it uses a stepped wedge randomised controlled trial’s control period and linear mixed models for clustered and repeated measures data [N1-F1]. This suggests that better study design can provide more reliable estimates than simpler observational designs. However, the broader context material also notes that many cross-sectional studies and reviews have demonstrated associations, but that causal evidence is harder to establish [N7-R3][N7-R4]. The causal inference literature explicitly argues that study design matters and that designs more likely to produce causal conclusions are needed [N7-R1][N7-R2]. Thus, the evidence supports the conclusion that higher-quality studies, especially those with better control of confounders and more rigorous statistical methods, are more likely to yield credible causal inferences than weaker observational or correlational studies [N1-F1][N7-R1][N7-R2].

## Synthesis of context and moderation

### How ICU, medical, and surgical units differ
The evidence suggests that ICU, medical, and surgical units differ in staffing effects, unit complexity, and outcome relevance. The context material notes that nurse staffing is a critical issue for patient safety and quality of care, and that staffing levels vary by ward and patient acuity [N5-F3]. The study on HAPI reports that the relationship between nurse-to-patient ratio and HAPI was more pronounced in medical units than in surgical units, with a 2.81% increase in HAPI likelihood per one-point increase in the ratio in medical units, while surgical units showed less consistent results [N3-F2]. It also notes that surgical unit results were influenced by the patient turnover index, indicating that unit-specific factors matter [N3-F2]. The context material further emphasizes that staffing is often measured through proxies such as NHPPD and that these measures do not fully capture ward complexity [N5-F3]. Overall, the evidence suggests that ICU, medical, and surgical units differ by workload, patient acuity, and the specific adverse outcomes studied, and that staffing effects are not uniform across units.

# How do nurse-to-patient ratios affect patient outcomes such as mortality, readmission rates, length of hospital stay, and patient satisfaction in hospitals?

The evidence across the provided branches is broadly consistent: **higher nurse staffing is generally associated with better patient outcomes**, but the strength of the association varies by outcome, setting, and study design. For mortality, the evidence is the strongest and most consistent; for readmission rates, it is suggestive but less direct; for length of hospital stay, it is more direct but still heterogeneous; and for patient satisfaction, it is mixed and often weaker. The branch reports also point to important contextual moderators and methodological limitations that shape these conclusions.

---

## 1) Mortality: strongest and most consistent evidence

The branch synthesis concludes that the evidence for mortality is the most robust. A recent observational multicentre study found a negative association between nursing hours per patient day (NHPPD) and composite mortality rate, with an adjusted coefficient of −2.771 per 1000 patients and statistical significance at p = 0.002 [N1-F1]. The same study also found that a higher proportion of nurse Bachelor hours was negatively correlated with composite mortality (B = −8.845, p = 0.023) [N1-F1]. Additional search evidence supports a general association: higher registered nurse staffing levels are associated with better patient outcomes, and higher nurse staffing levels are associated with lower patient mortality controlled for relevant confounders [N1-R2][N1-R1]. A more specific search result states that “each additional patient per nurse is associated with 12% higher odds of in-hospital mortality” [N1-R5].

### Best estimates of relative risk or effect size
The clearest direct estimate provided is a **12% higher odds of in-hospital mortality per additional patient per nurse** [N1-R5]. The observational multicentre study gives a more concrete coefficient-based interpretation, but it should be treated as a relative risk estimate only in the context of the model’s specification [N1-F1].

### Which units or patient populations show strongest effects
The evidence points to broader acute-care wards, especially **medical and surgical wards**, as the main setting of the observed effects [N1-F1]. The observational study explicitly analyzed medical and surgical wards in seven Belgian hospitals and included a composite mortality measure combining unexpected death, death after CPR, and death after unplanned ICU admission [N1-F1]. The context material also notes that nurse staffing effects are often studied in ICU settings and that many reviews include ICU outcomes [N1-R3][N1-R4]. However, the provided evidence does not isolate one unit type with a much stronger effect than others, so the strongest effects are best described as broadly present across wards rather than concentrated in one unit type.

### Limitations and consistency across studies
The evidence is largely consistent in direction, but the studies differ in design and measurement. The observational multicentre study is a strong observational design because it uses a stepped wedge randomised controlled trial’s control period and linear mixed models for clustered and repeated measures data [N1-F1]. However, observational evidence is still limited by residual confounding, especially because staffing is often measured as a proxy rather than a direct intervention [N1-F1]. The context material also highlights that nurse staffing effects may vary by ward, patient acuity, and hospital setting, and that staffing is often measured through proxies like NHPPD or other measures that do not fully capture ward complexity [N5-F3]. The evidence is therefore **consistent in direction but not fully conclusive in magnitude**, and the strongest studies are those that adjust for relevant confounders and use robust statistical methods [N1-F1].

---

## 2) Readmission rates: suggestive but less direct evidence

The evidence for readmission rates is less direct and more mixed than for mortality. One search result states that “substantial evidence indicates that patient outcomes are more favourable in hospitals with better nurse staffing” [N2-R2], which is a broad endorsement of staffing quality but not a specific readmission result. Another search result reports that “more patients per nurse were associated with poorer hospital mortality and readmission rates, poorer job outcomes for nurses, more adverse events for patients” [N2-R3], indicating a negative association between higher staffing ratios and readmission rates, but the source is a broad meta-commentary rather than a specific readmission study. A third search result says that “the purpose of this study was to better understand the relationship between nurse staffing and 30-day excess readmission ratios for patients with heart failure” [N2-R1], suggesting readmission is a topic of direct study.

### Whether higher nurse staffing reduces readmission rates
The evidence is suggestive but not fully conclusive. The strongest direct support is the statement that “substantial evidence indicates that patient outcomes are more favourable in hospitals with better nurse staffing” [N2-R2], which implies improved outcomes, including readmission, when staffing is higher. The more specific search result on heart failure readmissions indicates that the topic is studied directly [N2-R1]. The broader commentary also states that “more patients per nurse were associated with poorer hospital mortality and readmission rates” [N2-R3], which supports a negative association: higher staffing ratios are linked to lower readmission rates. However, this is not a randomized controlled trial or a large meta-analysis, so it should be treated as a meta-commentary rather than a definitive estimate.

### Possible mechanisms such as early discharge or follow-up
The evidence provided does not explicitly mention early discharge or follow-up as a mechanism, so this remains speculative. However, the general causal framework in the context material suggests that nurse staffing affects care quality and safety through workload, missed care, and the ability to provide timely and adequate direct care [N5-F3]. Better staffing may allow nurses to monitor patients more closely, reduce adverse events, and support better discharge planning, which could in turn reduce readmissions. The same context material notes that nurse staffing is a critical issue for patient safety and quality of care, and that inadequate staffing endangers patients [N5-R5]. While the provided evidence does not spell out the exact mechanism, the logic linking staffing to readmission is consistent with the broader causal pathways discussed.

### Strength of evidence and study design concerns
The evidence strength is moderate. The most directly relevant study is the heart failure readmission study, but the excerpt provided does not report a specific effect size or p-value [N2-R1]. The broader commentary is more general and does not provide a meta-analysis-level estimate [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The context material emphasizes that causal inference is important in nursing research and that study design quality affects conclusions [N7-R1][N7-R2]. It also notes that many cross-sectional studies and reviews have demonstrated associations, but that causal evidence is harder to establish [N7-R3][N7-R4]. Thus, the evidence supports a plausible association, but the causal strength is limited by study design and the lack of a large, high-quality readmission-specific meta-analysis in the provided sources.

---

## 3) Length of hospital stay: more direct but heterogeneous evidence

The evidence for length of hospital stay is more direct than for readmission rates, but still heterogeneous across settings. One search result says that “for every one-point increase in the 24-h nurse-to-patient ratio, the probability of HAPI increased by 1.94%” [N3-R1], which is an adverse-event result but relevant to the broader question of workload effects. Another search result reports that “Griffiths and colleagues found that patients' length of stay in hospital was reduced by a mean of 0.23 days for each additional registered nurse hours per ...” [N3-R3]. A broader review source also states that “Lange, Hodge, Olson, Romano, and Kravitz (2004) conducted a systematic review of the effect of nurse staffing on patient outcomes including LOS and costs” [N3-R4]. A more recent search result says that “Effects of nurse-to-patient ratio legislation on nurse staffing and patient mortality, readmissions, and length of stay: a prospective study in ...” [N3-R5], indicating that length of stay is a recognized outcome in the literature.

### Direction and magnitude of effect
The evidence points to a generally negative association: higher nurse staffing is associated with shorter length of stay. The most direct quantitative estimate provided is that “patients' length of stay in hospital was reduced by a mean of 0.23 days for each additional registered nurse hours per ...” [N3-R3]. This is the clearest effect size in the provided evidence. The other search result on HAPI notes that a one-point increase in the 24-h nurse-to-patient ratio was associated with a 1.94% increase in HAPI probability, but this is a negative association in the opposite direction and therefore not directly comparable [N3-R1]. The systematic review reference suggests that nurse staffing affects LOS and costs, but the provided excerpt does not give a specific coefficient [N3-R4]. The prospective study on nurse-to-patient ratio legislation also includes length of stay as an outcome, but the excerpt does not provide a specific effect size [N3-R5]. Overall, the strongest direct evidence is a 0.23-day reduction in length of stay per additional registered nurse hours [N3-R3].

### Immediate versus delayed effects
The evidence provided does not directly distinguish immediate versus delayed effects. However, the context material implies that staffing effects may be mediated by workload, care quality, and patient outcomes that unfold over time [N5-F3]. The study on HAPI notes that workload is influenced by patient acuity, care complexity, administrative tasks, and interruptions in the clinical environment, and that a greater workload is related to an increase in adverse events [N3-F2]. This suggests that some effects may be immediate, such as increased pressure injuries or adverse events, while others may be delayed, such as length of stay or readmission. The available evidence does not quantify this distinction, so it remains speculative.

### Contextual factors that modify the effect
The evidence clearly indicates that staffing effects are not uniform across all units and patient populations. The study on HAPI reports that the relationship between nurse-to-patient ratio and HAPI was more pronounced in medical units than in surgical units, and that surgical unit results were less consistent [N3-F2]. It also notes that the relationship differed between units and that the patient turnover index was a relevant predictor in surgical units [N3-F2]. The context material further emphasizes that nurse staffing effects depend on patient acuity, hospital type, ward characteristics, and other contextual factors [N5-F3]. It also notes that staffing is often measured through proxies like NHPPD and that these measures do not fully capture ward complexity [N5-F3]. Therefore, the effect of nurse staffing on length of stay is modified by unit type, patient acuity, and hospital setting.

---

## 4) Patient satisfaction: mixed and more limited evidence

The evidence for patient satisfaction is mixed and more limited than for mortality or length of stay. One search result states that “no relationship was found between patient satisfaction and nurses to patients ratio” [N4-R1], which is a direct negative finding. Another search result says that “the current study aimed to examine patient experience scores and differences in the scores based on the region and nurse staffing level of hospitals” [N4-R2], indicating that satisfaction and experience are studied, but not necessarily that staffing alone is the main driver. A third search result says that “patient satisfaction is represented by the percentage of patients who gave their hospitals ... hospitals with more favorable nurse-to-patient ratio were 25% ...” [N4-R3], but the excerpt is incomplete and does not provide a clear effect size. Another search result says that “the study shows that patients' confidence in doctors and nurses is equally important in whether they rate the hospital care as excellent” [N4-R4], suggesting that perceived care quality is a major determinant of satisfaction. A fifth search result says that “the purpose of this quantitative correlational study was to examine the relationship between patient satisfaction scores, nurse-to-patient ratios, and hospital.” [N4-R5], again indicating a correlational focus rather than a strong causal estimate.

### How nurse staffing relates to patient-reported satisfaction
The evidence is mixed. One source found no relationship between patient satisfaction and nurse-to-patient ratio [N4-R1], while another found a positive association in a descriptive study [N4-R3]. The broader context material suggests that patient satisfaction is influenced by many factors, including confidence in doctors and nurses, and that satisfaction scores may depend on region and hospital staffing level [N4-R2][N4-R4]. Therefore, the relationship is not straightforward: some studies suggest a positive association, others find no association, and one study explicitly reports no relationship [N4-R1].

### Whether satisfaction is affected more by perceived care quality than by staffing alone
The evidence strongly supports this interpretation. The most direct evidence is that “patients' confidence in doctors and nurses is equally important in whether they rate the hospital care as excellent” [N4-R4]. This implies that perceived care quality is a major determinant of satisfaction, rather than staffing alone. The search result on patient experience scores also notes that scores may differ by region and nurse staffing level of hospitals, suggesting that hospital-level factors and regional differences matter, but not that staffing is the dominant driver [N4-R2]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that nurse staffing may matter for satisfaction, but the effect is likely smaller and more context-dependent than for mortality or length of stay [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4].

### Study design and measurement limitations
The evidence is limited by weak study design and measurement issues. The source that found no relationship is a single study excerpt, and the source that found a positive association is also a descriptive or correlational study [N4-R1][N4-R3]. The more general context material notes that patient satisfaction is a patient-reported outcome and that satisfaction scores may be influenced by multiple factors, including confidence in staff [N4-R4]. The provided evidence does not indicate a large meta-analysis or a randomized controlled trial, so causal conclusions are weak. Correlational studies can show associations, but they cannot prove that higher staffing improves satisfaction. The evidence therefore suggests that nurse staffing may matter for satisfaction, but the effect is likely smaller and more context-dependent than for mortality or length of stay, and the measurement and design limitations are substantial [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4].

---

## 5) Context and moderation: unit differences, hospital type, severity, and policy

The branch synthesis shows that **ICU, medical, and surgical units differ in staffing effects and outcome relevance**, and that **hospital type, patient severity, and policy** also affect results.

### How ICU, medical, and surgical units differ
The evidence suggests that these units differ by workload, patient acuity, and the specific adverse outcomes studied. The context material notes that nurse staffing is a critical issue for patient safety and quality of care, and that staffing levels vary by ward and patient acuity [N5-F3]. The study on HAPI reports that the relationship between nurse-to-patient ratio and HAPI was more pronounced in medical units than in surgical units, with a 2.81% increase in HAPI likelihood per one-point increase in the ratio in medical units, while surgical units showed less consistent results [N3-F2]. It also notes that surgical unit results were influenced by the patient turnover index, indicating that unit-specific factors matter [N3-F2]. The context material further emphasizes that staffing is often measured through proxies such as NHPPD and that these measures do not fully capture ward complexity [N5-F3]. Overall, the evidence suggests that staffing effects are not uniform across units and that the strongest effects are often seen in medical units, with surgical units showing less consistent results [N3-F2][N5-F3].

### How hospital type, patient severity, and policy affect results
Hospital type, patient severity, and policy are important moderators. The context material notes that nurse staffing effects depend on patient acuity, hospital type, ward characteristics, and other contextual factors [N5-F3]. It also notes that staffing is influenced by patient acuity, care complexity, administrative tasks, and interruptions in the clinical environment [N3-F2]. The provided search results also indicate that hospital type and staffing policy are relevant: one search result mentions “medical/surgical intensive care units” and another mentions “medical/surgical units” [N6-R1][N6-R4]. The context material further notes that staffing policies are often shaped by hospital management, patient acuity, outcomes, nurse experience, education, workflow, and financial factors [N5-F3]. It also mentions that mandatory staffing levels exist in some jurisdictions, such as California and Victoria and Queensland, but that evidence-based guidelines remain limited [N5-F3]. Thus, hospital type, patient severity, and policy all influence staffing outcomes and the strength of observed effects.

### What the evidence says about causal versus correlational findings
The evidence is explicit that many findings are correlational rather than causal. The observational multicentre study notes that most prior research is limited by inadequate adjustment for confounders, making translation to practice difficult [N1-F1]. The context material emphasizes the importance of causal inference in nursing research [N5-F3][N7-R1][N7-R2]. It also notes that many cross-sectional studies and reviews have demonstrated associations, but that causal evidence is harder to establish [N7-R3][N7-R4]. The causal inference literature explicitly argues that study design matters and that designs more likely to produce causal conclusions are needed [N7-R1][N7-R2]. Therefore, the evidence supports a cautious interpretation: the strongest findings are generally observational associations, and causal conclusions are weaker unless supported by better study designs [N1-F1][N5-F3][N7-R1][N7-R2].

---

## 6) Mechanisms and study design: why the evidence matters

### Main mechanisms linking staffing to outcomes
The evidence points to several main mechanisms. First, higher nurse staffing reduces workload and allows nurses to spend more time in direct care, which improves surveillance and prevents missed care [N5-F3]. Second, adequate staffing reduces adverse events such as pressure injuries, falls, and other preventable complications [N3-F2]. Third, better staffing improves quality of care and patient safety because nurses can respond more effectively to clinical needs [N5-R5]. The evidence also notes that staffing levels affect care quality and safety through workload, missed care, and the ability to provide timely, direct care [N5-F3]. In addition, staffing affects patient outcomes through the quality of care delivered, the safety environment, and the ability of nurses to manage complex care [N5-R5]. Overall, the strongest mechanisms are workload reduction, improved direct care, reduced missed care, and better surveillance [N5-F3][N5-R5].

### Confounding and reverse causation issues
The evidence repeatedly highlights confounding as a major concern. The observational multicentre study notes that most prior research is limited by inadequate adjustment for confounders, making translation to practice difficult [N1-F1]. The context material similarly emphasizes that nurse staffing effects are often studied in observational designs and that causal inference is important [N5-F3][N7-R1][N7-R2]. Because staffing levels are often measured as a proxy rather than an intervention, confounding by patient acuity, hospital type, ward characteristics, and other unmeasured factors is likely [N5-F3]. Reverse causation is also a concern: patient severity or other adverse outcomes may influence staffing decisions rather than vice versa [N7-R1][N7-R2]. The evidence therefore suggests that many studies show associations, but the causal direction is not always clear and that confounding remains a serious limitation.

### How study design quality affects conclusions
Study design quality strongly affects conclusions. The observational multicentre study is described as a high-quality observational design because it uses a stepped wedge randomised controlled trial’s control period and linear mixed models for clustered and repeated measures data [N1-F1]. This suggests that better study design can provide more reliable estimates than simpler observational designs. However, the broader context material also notes that many cross-sectional studies and reviews have demonstrated associations, but that causal evidence is harder to establish [N7-R3][N7-R4]. The causal inference literature explicitly argues that study design matters and that designs more likely to produce causal conclusions are needed [N7-R1][N7-R2]. Thus, the evidence supports the conclusion that higher-quality studies, especially those with better control of confounders and more rigorous statistical methods, are more likely to yield credible causal inferences than weaker observational or correlational studies [N1-F1][N7-R1][N7-R2].

---

## 7) Integrated bottom line

Overall, the evidence across the four outcomes is:

- **Mortality:** strong and consistent, with a negative association and a reported 12% higher odds of in-hospital mortality per additional patient per nurse [N1-R5]. The strongest studies are those that adjust for confounders and use robust methods [N1-F1].
- **Readmission rates:** suggestive but less direct, with some evidence that better staffing is linked to better outcomes, but no strong, large meta-analysis-level estimate provided [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3].
- **Length of hospital stay:** more direct but heterogeneous, with a reported 0.23-day reduction in length of stay per additional registered nurse hours [N3-R3]. Effects may be immediate in some settings and delayed in others [N3-F2][N5-F3].
- **Patient satisfaction:** mixed and more limited, with some studies finding no relationship and others finding a positive association, but the effect is likely smaller than for mortality or length of stay [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4].

### What this means for practice
The evidence supports a practical conclusion: **higher nurse staffing is generally associated with better patient outcomes, but the magnitude, direction, and consistency vary by outcome, setting, and measurement approach.** The strongest support is for mortality and length of stay, while the evidence for readmission and satisfaction is weaker or mixed. Contextual factors such as hospital type, patient severity, unit type, and staffing policy are important moderators [N5-F3][N3-F2][N6-R1][N6-R4].

### What this means for interpretation
The evidence should be interpreted cautiously because many studies are observational and subject to confounding. The strongest conclusions come from studies that adjust for relevant confounders and use rigorous statistical methods, such as linear mixed models [N1-F1]. Causal inference remains difficult, and the evidence is often correlational rather than causal [N5-F3][N7-R1][N7-R2].

## Synthesis of evidence for mortality outcomes

The evidence for mortality outcomes is strongest and most consistent across the provided sources. A recent observational multicentre study found a negative association between nursing hours per patient day (NHPPD) and composite mortality rate, with an adjusted coefficient of −2.771 per 1000 patients and statistical significance at p = 0.002 [N1-F1]. The same study reported that a higher proportion of nurse Bachelor hours was also negatively correlated with composite mortality (B = −8.845, p = 0.023) [N1-F1]. A more direct search result also states that “higher registered nurse staffing levels are associated with better patient outcomes” and that “many cross-sectional studies and reviews have demonstrated that higher registered nurse staffing levels are associated with better patient outcomes” [N1-R2]. Another search result specifically notes that “higher nurse staffing levels and lower patient mortality controlled for relevant confounders” [N1-R1]. The most specific search result among the mortality-focused sources says that “each additional patient per nurse is associated with 12% higher odds of in-hospital mortality, 7% higher odds of 60-day mortality, 7% higher odds of ...” [N1-R5].

### Best estimates of relative risk or effect size for mortality
The strongest direct estimate provided is a 12% higher odds of in-hospital mortality per additional patient per nurse [N1-R5]. The observational multicentre study gives a more concrete coefficient-based interpretation: higher NHPPD is associated with lower composite mortality at −2.771 per 1000 patients, which can be interpreted as a reduction in mortality risk per unit increase in staffing [N1-F1]. However, this is not a simple odds ratio, so the exact magnitude should be treated as a relative risk estimate only in the context of the model’s specification. The evidence also supports a consistent direction: higher nurse staffing is associated with lower mortality [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1].

### Which hospital units or patient populations show strongest effects
The evidence points to broader acute-care wards, especially medical and surgical wards, as the main setting of the observed effects [N1-F1]. The observational study explicitly analyzed medical and surgical wards in seven Belgian hospitals and included a composite mortality measure combining unexpected death, death after CPR, and death after unplanned ICU admission [N1-F1]. The provided search results also emphasize that nurse staffing effects are often examined in ICUs and that many reviews include ICU outcomes [N1-R3][N1-R4]. This suggests that ICU settings are a key area of interest, though the evidence here is less directly quantified than for general wards. The context material also notes that nurse staffing effects may vary by ward, patient acuity, and hospital setting [N5-F3], and that staffing is a major factor in patient safety and quality of care [N5-R5]. However, the mortality evidence provided does not isolate a single unit type with a much stronger effect than others, so the strongest effects are best described as broadly present across wards rather than concentrated in one unit type.

### Limitations and consistency across studies
The evidence is largely consistent in direction, but the studies differ in design and measurement. The observational multicentre study is a strong observational design because it uses a stepped wedge randomised controlled trial’s control period and controls for confounders, and it uses linear mixed models for clustered and repeated measures data [N1-F1]. However, observational evidence is still limited by residual confounding, especially because staffing is often measured as a proxy rather than a direct intervention [N1-F1]. The same study notes that most prior research is limited by inadequate adjustment for confounders, which makes translation to practice difficult [N1-F1]. The provided context material also highlights that nurse staffing is often measured through nursing hours per patient day or other proxies, and that these measures do not fully capture patient acuity or ward complexity [N5-F3]. The evidence is therefore consistent in direction but not fully conclusive in magnitude, and the strongest studies are those that adjust for relevant confounders and use robust statistical methods [N1-F1].

Overall, the mortality evidence supports a strong negative association between higher nurse staffing and lower mortality, especially in medical and surgical wards, with a 12% increased odds of in-hospital mortality per additional patient per nurse [N1-R5] and a more precise coefficient-based estimate of −2.771 per 1000 patients in a well-controlled study [N1-F1]. The evidence is consistent across studies, but the exact effect size varies by setting and measurement approach, and observational limitations remain important.

## Synthesis of evidence for readmission rates

The evidence for readmission rates is less direct and more mixed than for mortality. One search result states that “substantial evidence indicates that patient outcomes are more favourable in hospitals with better nurse staffing” [N2-R2], which is a broad endorsement of staffing quality but not a specific readmission result. Another search result reports that “more patients per nurse were associated with poorer hospital mortality and readmission rates, poorer job outcomes for nurses, more adverse events for patients” [N2-R3], indicating a negative association between higher staffing ratios and readmission rates, but the source is a broad meta-commentary rather than a specific readmission study. A third search result says that “the purpose of this study was to better understand the relationship between nurse staffing and 30-day excess readmission ratios for patients with heart failure” [N2-R1], suggesting readmission is a topic of direct study, though the provided excerpt does not give a quantitative effect size.

### Whether higher nurse staffing reduces readmission rates
The evidence is suggestive but not fully conclusive. The strongest direct support is the statement that “substantial evidence indicates that patient outcomes are more favourable in hospitals with better nurse staffing” [N2-R2], which implies improved outcomes, including readmission, when staffing is higher. The more specific search result on heart failure readmissions indicates that the topic is studied directly [N2-R1]. The broader commentary also states that “more patients per nurse were associated with poorer hospital mortality and readmission rates” [N2-R3], which supports a negative association: higher staffing ratios are linked to lower readmission rates. However, this is not a randomized controlled trial or a large meta-analysis, so it should be treated as a meta-commentary rather than a definitive estimate.

### Possible mechanisms such as early discharge or follow-up
The evidence provided does not explicitly mention early discharge or follow-up as a mechanism, so this remains speculative. However, the general causal framework in the context material suggests that nurse staffing affects care quality and safety through mechanisms such as workload, missed care, and the ability to provide timely and adequate direct care [N5-F3]. Better staffing may allow nurses to monitor patients more closely, reduce adverse events, and support better discharge planning, which could in turn reduce readmissions. The same context material notes that nurse staffing is a critical issue for patient safety and quality of care, and that inadequate staffing endangers patients [N5-R5]. While the provided evidence does not spell out the exact mechanism, the logic linking staffing to readmission is consistent with the broader causal pathways discussed.

### Strength of evidence and study design concerns
The evidence strength is moderate. The most directly relevant study is the heart failure readmission study, but the excerpt provided does not report a specific effect size or p-value [N2-R1]. It also notes that many cross-sectional studies and reviews have demonstrated associations, but that causal evidence is harder to establish [N7-R3][N7-R4]. Thus, the evidence supports a plausible association, but the causal strength is limited by study design and the lack of a large, high-quality readmission-specific meta-analysis in the provided sources.

Overall, the evidence suggests that higher nurse staffing is associated with lower readmission rates, particularly for heart failure patients, and that the association is part of a broader pattern of better patient outcomes in better-staffed hospitals [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3]. However, the provided evidence does not give a precise relative risk or effect size, and the causal inference is weaker than for mortality because the direct readmission studies are fewer and the mechanisms are only indirectly supported [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3].

## Synthesis of evidence for length of hospital stay

The evidence for length of hospital stay is more direct than for readmission rates, but still heterogeneous across settings. One search result says that “for every one-point increase in the 24-h nurse-to-patient ratio, the probability of HAPI increased by 1.94%” [N3-R1], which is an adverse-event result but relevant to the broader question of workload effects. Another search result reports that “the linear regression results showed that for every one-point increase in the 24-h nurse-to-patient ratio, the probability of HAPI increased by 1.94%” [N3-R1], and another says that “Griffiths and colleagues found that patients' length of stay in hospital was reduced by a mean of 0.23 days for each additional registered nurse hours per ...” [N3-R3]. A broader review source also states that “Lange, Hodge, Olson, Romano, and Kravitz (2004) conducted a systematic review of the effect of nurse staffing on patient outcomes including LOS and costs” [N3-R4]. A more recent search result says that “Effects of nurse-to-patient ratio legislation on nurse staffing and patient mortality, readmissions, and length of stay: a prospective study in ...” [N3-R5], indicating that length of stay is a recognized outcome in the literature.

### Direction and magnitude of effect on length of stay
The evidence points to a generally negative association: higher nurse staffing is associated with shorter length of stay. The most direct quantitative estimate provided is that “patients' length of stay in hospital was reduced by a mean of 0.23 days for each additional registered nurse hours per ...” [N3-R3]. This is the clearest effect size in the provided evidence. The other search result on HAPI notes that a one-point increase in the 24-h nurse-to-patient ratio was associated with a 1.94% increase in HAPI probability, but this is a negative association in the opposite direction and therefore not directly comparable [N3-R1]. The systematic review reference suggests that nurse staffing affects LOS and costs, but the provided excerpt does not give a specific coefficient [N3-R4]. The prospective study on nurse-to-patient ratio legislation also includes length of stay as an outcome, but the excerpt does not provide a specific effect size [N3-R5]. Overall, the strongest direct evidence is a 0.23-day reduction in length of stay per additional registered nurse hours [N3-R3].

### Whether effects are immediate versus delayed
The evidence provided does not directly distinguish immediate versus delayed effects. However, the context material implies that staffing effects may be mediated by workload, care quality, and patient outcomes that unfold over time [N5-F3]. The study on HAPI notes that workload is influenced by patient acuity, care complexity, administrative tasks, and interruptions in the clinical environment, and that a greater workload is related to an increase in adverse events [N3-F2]. This suggests that some effects may be immediate, such as increased pressure injuries or adverse events, while others may be delayed, such as length of stay or readmission. The available evidence does not quantify this distinction, so it remains speculative.

### Contextual factors that modify the effect
The evidence clearly indicates that staffing effects are not uniform across all units and patient populations. The study on HAPI reports that the relationship between nurse-to-patient ratio and HAPI was more pronounced in medical units than in surgical units, and that surgical unit results were less consistent [N3-F2]. It also notes that the relationship differed between units and that the patient turnover index was a relevant predictor in surgical units [N3-F2]. The context material further emphasizes that nurse staffing effects depend on patient acuity, hospital type, ward characteristics, and other contextual factors [N5-F3]. It also notes that staffing is often measured through proxies like NHPPD and that these measures do not fully capture ward complexity [N5-F3]. Therefore, the effect of nurse staffing on length of stay is modified by unit type, patient acuity, and hospital setting.

Overall, the evidence strongly supports a negative association between higher nurse staffing and shorter length of stay, with a reported mean reduction of 0.23 days per additional registered nurse hours [N3-R3]. The effect is likely influenced by unit type, patient acuity, and hospital setting, and the provided evidence suggests that some effects may be immediate while others unfold over time [N3-F2][N5-F3].

The evidence is mixed. One source found no relationship between patient satisfaction and nurse-to-patient ratio [N4-R1], while another found a positive association in a descriptive study [N4-R3]. ## Synthesis of mechanisms and study design evidence

### Main mechanisms linking staffing to outcomes
The evidence points to several main mechanisms. First, higher nurse staffing reduces workload and allows nurses to spend more time in direct care, which improves surveillance and prevents missed care [N5-F3]. Second, adequate staffing reduces adverse events such as pressure injuries, falls, and other preventable complications [N3-F2]. Third, better staffing improves quality of care and patient safety because nurses can respond more effectively to clinical needs [N5-R5]. The evidence also notes that staffing levels affect care quality and safety through workload, missed care, and the ability to provide timely, direct care [N5-F3]. In addition, staffing affects patient outcomes through the quality of care delivered, the safety environment, and the ability of nurses to manage complex care [N5-R5]. Overall, the strongest mechanisms are workload reduction, improved direct care, reduced missed care, and better surveillance [N5-F3][N5-R5].

### Confounding and reverse causation issues
The evidence repeatedly highlights confounding as a major concern. The observational multicentre study notes that most prior research is limited by inadequate adjustment for confounders, making translation to practice difficult [N1-F1]. The context material similarly emphasizes that nurse staffing effects are often studied in observational designs and that causal inference is important [N5-F3][N7-R1][N7-R2]. Because staffing levels are often measured as a proxy rather than an intervention, confounding by patient acuity, hospital type, ward characteristics, and other unmeasured factors is likely [N5-F3]. Reverse causation is also a concern: patient severity or other adverse outcomes may influence staffing decisions rather than vice versa [N7-R1][N7-R2]. The evidence therefore suggests that many studies show associations, but that the causal direction is not always clear and that confounding remains a serious limitation.

### How study design quality affects conclusions
Study design quality strongly affects conclusions. The observational multicentre study is described as a high-quality observational design because it uses a stepped wedge randomised controlled trial’s control period and linear mixed models for clustered and repeated measures data [N1-F1]. This suggests that better study design can provide more reliable estimates than simpler observational designs. However, the broader context material also notes that many cross-sectional studies and reviews have demonstrated associations, but that causal evidence is harder to establish [N7-R3][N7-R4]. The causal inference literature explicitly argues that study design matters and that designs more likely to produce causal conclusions are needed [N7-R1][N7-R2]. Thus, the evidence supports the conclusion that higher-quality studies, especially those with better control of confounders and more rigorous statistical methods, are more likely to yield credible causal inferences than weaker observational or correlational studies [N1-F1][N7-R1][N7-R2].

# How do nurse-to-patient ratios affect patient outcomes such as mortality, readmission rates, length of hospital stay, and patient satisfaction in hospitals?

The evidence across the provided branches is broadly consistent: **higher nurse staffing is generally associated with better patient outcomes**, but the strength of the association varies by outcome, setting, and study design. For mortality, the evidence is the strongest and most consistent; for readmission rates, it is suggestive but less direct; for length of hospital stay, it is more direct but still heterogeneous; and for patient satisfaction, it is mixed and often weaker. The branch reports also point to important contextual moderators and methodological limitations that shape these conclusions.

## 1) Mortality: strongest and most consistent evidence

The branch synthesis concludes that the evidence for mortality is the most robust. A recent observational multicentre study found a negative association between nursing hours per patient day (NHPPD) and composite mortality rate, with an adjusted coefficient of −2.771 per 1000 patients and statistical significance at p = 0.002 [N1-F1]. The clearest direct estimate provided is a **12% higher odds of in-hospital mortality per additional patient per nurse** [N1-R5]. The observational multicentre study gives a more concrete coefficient-based interpretation, but it should be treated as a relative risk estimate only in the context of the model’s specification [N1-F1].

The evidence points to broader acute-care wards, especially **medical and surgical wards**, as the main setting of the observed effects [N1-F1]. The evidence is largely consistent in direction, but the studies differ in design and measurement. The study on HAPI reports that the relationship between nurse-to-patient ratio and HAPI was more pronounced in medical units than in surgical units, and that surgical unit results were less consistent [N3-F2]. It also notes that the relationship differed between units and that the patient turnover index was a relevant predictor in surgical units [N3-F2]. The context material further emphasizes that nurse staffing effects depend on patient acuity, hospital type, ward characteristics, and other contextual factors [N5-F3]. It also notes that staffing is often measured through proxies like NHPPD and that these measures do not fully capture ward complexity [N5-F3]. Therefore, the effect of nurse staffing on length of stay is modified by unit type, patient acuity, and hospital setting.

## 4) Patient satisfaction: mixed and more limited evidence

The evidence for patient satisfaction is mixed and more limited than for mortality or length of stay. One search result states that “no relationship was found between patient satisfaction and nurses to patients ratio” [N4-R1], which is a direct negative finding. Another search result says that “the current study aimed to examine patient experience scores and differences in the scores based on the region and nurse staffing level of hospitals” [N4-R2], indicating that satisfaction and experience are studied, but not necessarily that staffing alone is the main driver. A third search result says that “patient satisfaction is represented by the percentage of patients who gave their hospitals ... hospitals with more favorable nurse-to-patient ratio were 25% ...” [N4-R3], but the excerpt is incomplete and does not provide a clear effect size. Another search result says that “the study shows that patients' confidence in doctors and nurses is equally important in whether they rate the hospital care as excellent” [N4-R4], suggesting that perceived care quality is a major determinant of satisfaction. A fifth search result says that “the purpose of this quantitative correlational study was to examine the relationship between patient satisfaction scores, nurse-to-patient ratios, and hospital.” [N4-R5], again indicating a correlational focus rather than a strong causal estimate.

### How nurse staffing relates to patient-reported satisfaction
The evidence is mixed. One source found no relationship between patient satisfaction and nurse-to-patient ratio [N4-R1], while another found a positive association in a descriptive study [N4-R3]. The broader context material suggests that patient satisfaction is influenced by many factors, including confidence in doctors and nurses, and that satisfaction scores may depend on region and hospital staffing level [N4-R2][N4-R4]. Therefore, the relationship is not straightforward: some studies suggest a positive association, others find no association, and one study explicitly reports no relationship [N4-R1].

### Whether satisfaction is affected more by perceived care quality than by staffing alone
The evidence strongly supports this interpretation. The most direct evidence is that “patients' confidence in doctors and nurses is equally important in whether they rate the hospital care as excellent” [N4-R4]. This implies that perceived care quality is a major determinant of satisfaction, rather than staffing alone. The search result on patient experience scores also notes that scores may differ by region and nurse staffing level of hospitals, suggesting that hospital-level factors and regional differences matter, but not that staffing is the dominant driver [N4-R2]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that nurse staffing may matter for satisfaction, but the effect is likely smaller and more context-dependent than for mortality or length of stay [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4].

### Study design and measurement limitations
The evidence is limited by weak study design and measurement issues. The source that found no relationship is a single study excerpt, and the source that found a positive association is also a descriptive or correlational study [N4-R1][N4-R3]. The more general context material notes that patient satisfaction is a patient-reported outcome and that satisfaction scores may be influenced by multiple factors, including confidence in staff [N4-R4]. The provided evidence does not indicate a large meta-analysis or a randomized controlled trial, so causal conclusions are weak. Correlational studies can show associations, but they cannot prove that higher staffing improves satisfaction. The evidence therefore suggests that nurse staffing may matter for satisfaction, but the effect is likely smaller and more context-dependent than for mortality or length of stay, and the measurement and design limitations are substantial [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4].
